primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Pseudohypoparathyroidism results from impaired PTH/PTHrP signaling, commonly involving GNAS. In the classic Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype, reduced Gs-alpha signaling causes end-organ resistance to PTH, producing hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH despite intact hormone production.
vignette: A 14-year-old girl is evaluated for intermittent muscle cramps. She has short stature, obesity, a round face, and shortening of the fourth metacarpals. Laboratory studies show low serum calcium, high serum phosphate, and elevated parathyroid hormone concentration. Renal function is normal.
lead: Which cellular signaling abnormality most directly explains these findings?
correct: Reduced Gs-alpha–mediated cyclic AMP signaling in target tissues
distractors: Constitutive activation of the calcium-sensing receptor in parathyroid cells
Loss of MEN1-dependent transcriptional regulation in parathyroid tissue
Activating mutation of the stimulatory G-protein in thyroid follicular cells
Impaired conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D in proximal tubules
distractor_notes: Activating calcium-sensing receptor variants can cause hypocalcemia with inappropriately low or normal PTH, not elevated PTH with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
MEN1 loss predisposes to primary hyperparathyroidism with elevated calcium rather than PTH resistance with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.
Activating Gs-alpha signaling is associated with conditions such as McCune-Albright syndrome and would not explain hormone resistance.
Reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylation may cause hypocalcemia but does not explain the Albright phenotype or the characteristic PTH-resistance pattern.
key_expl: The phenotype of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy plus hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated PTH indicates pseudohypoparathyroidism. The core defect is reduced Gs-alpha/cAMP signaling downstream of the PTH receptor, most commonly from GNAS-related abnormalities.
objective: Recognize pseudohypoparathyroidism and connect elevated PTH with hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and Albright hereditary osteodystrophy to impaired Gs-alpha/cAMP signaling.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Biallelic MTTP loss prevents lipidation of nascent apolipoprotein B in enterocytes and hepatocytes, blocking formation of chylomicrons and VLDL. The result is fat malabsorption, extremely low apoB-containing lipoproteins, acanthocytosis, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
vignette: A 7-year-old boy has chronic steatorrhea, poor growth, progressive gait instability, and diminished vibration sensation. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous acanthocytes. Serum triglyceride and LDL cholesterol concentrations are extremely low, and plasma apolipoprotein B is undetectable.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
distractors: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Familial hypercholesterolemia
Cholestatic fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
Tangier disease
distractor_notes: Familial chylomicronemia causes markedly elevated triglycerides from impaired lipoprotein lipase pathway function, the opposite of the very low apoB-containing lipoproteins here.
Familial hypercholesterolemia causes markedly elevated LDL cholesterol rather than undetectable apoB and steatorrhea.
Cholestasis can cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiency but would not explain absent apoB-containing lipoproteins and the characteristic acanthocytosis.
Tangier disease is caused by ABCA1 dysfunction with extremely low HDL cholesterol and cholesterol ester accumulation, not absent apoB-containing lipoproteins.
key_expl: Steatorrhea, acanthocytes, neurologic manifestations of fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and nearly absent LDL/triglycerides/apoB are classic for abetalipoproteinemia caused by MTTP deficiency.
objective: Recognize abetalipoproteinemia from fat malabsorption, acanthocytosis, neurologic vitamin E deficiency, and absent apoB-containing lipoproteins.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: ATP7A encodes a copper-transporting P-type ATPase required for normal cellular copper handling and systemic copper distribution. Severe ATP7A dysfunction produces copper deficiency in multiple tissues, impairing copper-dependent enzymes and causing neurodegeneration, connective-tissue abnormalities, and characteristic pili torti hair.
vignette: A 4-month-old boy has failure to thrive, hypotonia, and new-onset seizures. His scalp hair is sparse, lightly pigmented, and unusually twisted; microscopy shows pili torti. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are low.
lead: Which molecular defect most directly explains this disorder?
correct: Loss of function of an ATP-dependent copper-transporting membrane protein
distractors: Loss of function of a copper-transporting ATPase responsible for biliary copper excretion
Deficiency of lysyl oxidase caused by an isolated autosomal recessive enzyme mutation
Defective heme synthesis due to reduced ferrochelatase activity
Failure of intestinal zinc uptake through the ZIP4 transporter
distractor_notes: ATP7B dysfunction causes Wilson disease through impaired biliary copper excretion and copper accumulation rather than systemic copper deficiency with kinky hair in infancy.
Reduced lysyl oxidase activity is one consequence of copper deficiency, but the primary defect in Menkes disease is ATP7A-mediated copper transport.
Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria and does not explain low copper, low ceruloplasmin, and pili torti.
ZIP4 dysfunction causes acrodermatitis enteropathica with zinc deficiency, dermatitis, alopecia, and diarrhea rather than the Menkes neurologic and hair phenotype.
key_expl: Classic Menkes disease presents after an initially normal neonatal period with neurodegeneration, seizures, failure to thrive, and kinky or pili torti hair. It is caused by pathogenic variants in ATP7A, which encodes a copper-transporting ATPase.
objective: Connect the classic infantile Menkes phenotype to ATP7A-dependent copper transport failure.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
outline: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: ABCD1 encodes a peroxisomal ATP-binding cassette transporter that moves very-long-chain fatty-acid substrates into peroxisomes. Loss of ABCD1 function impairs peroxisomal beta-oxidation and causes accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, affecting cerebral white matter and adrenal cortex.
vignette: A previously healthy 7-year-old boy develops progressive school difficulty, behavioral changes, spastic gait, and visual impairment. MRI shows symmetric posterior cerebral white-matter demyelination. He also has hyperpigmentation and low morning cortisol with elevated ACTH. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids are increased.
lead: Which cellular process is most directly impaired?
correct: Transport of very-long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes for beta-oxidation
distractors: Transport of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria by the carnitine shuttle
Alpha-oxidation of branched-chain phytanic acid within peroxisomes
Mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids
Lysosomal hydrolysis of sphingomyelin to ceramide
distractor_notes: Carnitine-shuttle defects impair mitochondrial oxidation of long-chain fatty acids and cause fasting intolerance or myopathy rather than cerebral demyelination with adrenal insufficiency and elevated VLCFAs.
Defective phytanic acid alpha-oxidation causes Refsum disease, typically with retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy, ataxia, and ichthyosis.
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia and does not produce elevated VLCFAs or progressive cerebral demyelination.
Sphingomyelinase deficiency causes Niemann-Pick disease, not the X-ALD adrenal and VLCFA phenotype.
key_expl: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy combines neurologic disease with adrenal cortical dysfunction. ABCD1 loss prevents normal peroxisomal import of certain VLCFAs, impairing their beta-oxidation and causing VLCFA accumulation.
objective: Recognize X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and identify defective peroxisomal VLCFA transport/beta-oxidation as the underlying process.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Familial Mediterranean fever is an inherited autoinflammatory disorder caused by pathogenic variants in MEFV encoding pyrin, leading to inappropriate inflammasome-driven inflammation and recurrent short attacks of fever and serositis. Untreated chronic inflammation can cause AA amyloidosis.
vignette: A 19-year-old man of Armenian ancestry has had recurrent attacks of fever with severe diffuse abdominal pain since childhood. Each episode lasts about 1 to 2 days and resolves completely without treatment. Between attacks he feels well. Several relatives have similar episodes, and one uncle developed renal failure from AA amyloidosis.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this pattern?
distractors: Systemic lupus erythematosus
Acute intermittent porphyria
Hereditary angioedema
Adult-onset Still disease
distractor_notes: Systemic lupus erythematosus can cause serositis but usually has additional autoimmune features and does not characteristically cause lifelong stereotyped 1- to 3-day attacks with complete wellness between episodes.
Acute intermittent porphyria causes neurovisceral attacks but not recurrent febrile serositis and AA amyloidosis.
Hereditary angioedema causes episodic edema and abdominal pain without urticaria, but fever and inflammatory serositis are not characteristic.
Adult-onset Still disease typically causes quotidian fever, inflammatory arthritis, and an evanescent rash rather than childhood-onset brief recurrent serositis with a strong familial pattern.
key_expl: Brief self-limited attacks of fever and peritonitis beginning in childhood, Mediterranean ancestry, a family history, and AA amyloidosis are classic for familial Mediterranean fever due to MEFV/pyrin pathway dysfunction.
objective: Recognize familial Mediterranean fever from recurrent short attacks of fever and serositis and connect the disease to MEFV/pyrin-mediated autoinflammation.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
discipline: Pathology / Immunology / Genetics / Histology & Cell Biology
mechanism: An acquired somatic PIGA mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell impairs synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor. Loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators such as CD55 and CD59 makes blood cells abnormally susceptible to complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis and thrombosis.
vignette: A 32-year-old man has episodic dark urine, fatigue, abdominal pain, and a prior hepatic-vein thrombosis. Laboratory studies show Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis. Flow cytometry demonstrates a population of blood cells lacking CD55 and CD59.
lead: Which molecular abnormality most directly causes this disease?
correct: Somatic PIGA mutation causing failure to synthesize GPI membrane anchors
distractors: Germline mutation causing spectrin deficiency in erythrocyte membranes
Autoantibodies against erythrocyte Rh antigens
Loss of ADAMTS13 activity due to an acquired inhibitor
Factor V mutation causing resistance to activated protein C
distractor_notes: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis with extravascular hemolysis and spherocytes, not loss of CD55/CD59.
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia can involve Rh-directed antibodies and a positive direct antiglobulin test, unlike PNH.
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with microangiopathic hemolysis and thrombocytopenia, not GPI-anchor loss.
Factor V Leiden increases thrombosis risk but does not cause complement-mediated hemolysis or loss of CD55/CD59.
key_expl: PNH is an acquired clonal stem-cell disorder caused by somatic PIGA mutation. Defective GPI anchors prevent expression of complement-regulatory proteins including CD55 and CD59, producing intravascular hemolysis and unusual-site thrombosis.
objective: Connect Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, unusual venous thrombosis, and absent CD55/CD59 to an acquired PIGA-mediated GPI-anchor defect.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Hereditary orotic aciduria due to UMP synthase deficiency
mechanism: UMP synthase is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes the last two steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis: conversion of orotate to orotidine monophosphate and then to UMP. Deficiency causes orotic acid accumulation and impaired pyrimidine availability, producing megaloblastic anemia that does not respond to folate or vitamin B12; unlike OTC deficiency, hyperammonemia is absent.
vignette: A 9-month-old infant has failure to thrive and persistent macrocytic anemia despite adequate folate and vitamin B12. Urine contains abundant orotic acid crystals. Plasma ammonia concentration is normal.
lead: Deficiency of which enzyme most directly explains these findings?
distractors: Ornithine transcarbamylase
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase
Adenosine deaminase
distractor_notes: OTC deficiency can increase orotic acid because excess carbamoyl phosphate enters pyrimidine synthesis, but it characteristically causes hyperammonemia.
CPS I deficiency causes hyperammonemia with low or normal orotic acid rather than marked hereditary orotic aciduria.
Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase participates earlier in pyrimidine synthesis; its dysfunction is associated with Miller syndrome rather than the classic hereditary orotic aciduria phenotype.
Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic purine metabolite accumulation, not isolated orotic aciduria and megaloblastic anemia.
key_expl: Megaloblastic anemia refractory to vitamin replacement plus marked orotic aciduria without hyperammonemia identifies hereditary orotic aciduria from UMP synthase deficiency, not a urea-cycle defect.
objective: Differentiate hereditary orotic aciduria from urea-cycle disorders and identify UMP synthase as the defective enzyme.

outline: Epithelial sodium channel gain of function
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Gain-of-function variants affecting ENaC subunits reduce channel degradation or increase channel activity in the distal nephron. Excess sodium reabsorption expands extracellular volume, suppresses renin and aldosterone, and promotes potassium and hydrogen ion secretion, causing hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis.
vignette: A 21-year-old man has severe hypertension despite no obesity or renal artery disease. His father developed hypertension in his twenties. Laboratory studies show potassium 2.9 mEq/L, bicarbonate 33 mEq/L, suppressed plasma renin activity, and low aldosterone concentration.
lead: Which abnormality most directly causes this patient's hypertension?
correct: Gain of function of the epithelial sodium channel in the distal nephron
distractors: Constitutive activation of the mineralocorticoid receptor by aldosterone excess
Loss of function of the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter
Loss of function of the renal outer medullary potassium channel
Increased renin secretion from juxtaglomerular cells
distractor_notes: Primary aldosteronism causes similar hypertension and hypokalemia but has elevated aldosterone rather than suppressed aldosterone.
Loss of the NaCl cotransporter causes Gitelman syndrome with salt wasting and low or normal blood pressure.
ROMK loss causes a Bartter phenotype with renal salt wasting rather than volume-expanded hypertension.
Increased renin would raise aldosterone and is inconsistent with the suppressed renin and aldosterone shown.
key_expl: Early-onset familial hypertension with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis and suppression of both renin and aldosterone is classic for Liddle syndrome, caused by ENaC gain of function. ENaC blockers such as amiloride directly target the defect.
objective: Recognize Liddle syndrome and connect low-renin/low-aldosterone hypertension with hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis to ENaC gain of function.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia is an autosomal dominant vascular dysplasia most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in ENG or ACVRL1, genes in TGF-beta/BMP signaling pathways. Patients form mucocutaneous telangiectases and arteriovenous malformations that lack an intervening capillary bed.
vignette: A 36-year-old woman has recurrent spontaneous epistaxis and iron-deficiency anemia. Examination shows multiple small blanching telangiectases on the lips, tongue, and fingertips. Her father had similar nosebleeds and was treated for a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
distractors: Ataxia-telangiectasia
CREST syndrome
von Willebrand disease
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
distractor_notes: Ataxia-telangiectasia causes childhood cerebellar ataxia, immunodeficiency, and conjunctival/cutaneous telangiectases rather than an autosomal dominant pattern of epistaxis and visceral AVMs.
CREST syndrome can cause facial and hand telangiectases but would be accompanied by systemic sclerosis features and does not explain familial pulmonary AVMs.
von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding but not characteristic telangiectases or AVMs.
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes can cause vascular fragility in selected subtypes but not the classic mucocutaneous telangiectasia plus visceral AVM pattern.
key_expl: Recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectases, visceral AVMs, and autosomal dominant transmission identify hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. ENG and ACVRL1 account for most molecularly defined cases.
objective: Recognize hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia from recurrent epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectases, visceral AVMs, and autosomal dominant inheritance.

outline: Alpha-3 type IV collagen NC1 autoantigen
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Goodpasture syndrome is caused by autoantibodies directed primarily against the noncollagenous NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, a shared basement-membrane component in glomerular and pulmonary alveolar capillaries. Immunofluorescence shows linear IgG along the GBM.
vignette: A 24-year-old man develops hemoptysis, dyspnea, hematuria, and rapidly rising serum creatinine. Urinalysis shows red blood cell casts. Kidney biopsy reveals crescentic glomerulonephritis, and immunofluorescence shows smooth linear IgG deposition along glomerular capillary basement membranes.
lead: The pathogenic autoantibodies are directed primarily against which target?
correct: NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen
distractors: Alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane
Proteinase 3 within neutrophil azurophilic granules
Myeloperoxidase within neutrophil lysosomes
Phospholipase A2 receptor on podocytes
distractor_notes: COL4A5 abnormalities cause X-linked Alport syndrome; they are inherited structural defects, not the principal autoantigen of anti-GBM disease.
PR3-ANCA is associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which typically produces pauci-immune rather than linear-IgG glomerulonephritis.
MPO-ANCA is associated with microscopic polyangiitis and other pauci-immune vasculitides, not classic linear anti-GBM deposition.
PLA2R is a major target antigen in primary membranous nephropathy, which causes nephrotic syndrome rather than pulmonary-renal crescentic disease.
key_expl: Pulmonary hemorrhage plus rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with linear GBM IgG is anti-GBM disease. The classic autoantigen is the noncollagenous NC1 domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, which is present in both glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
objective: Identify the alpha-3 type IV collagen NC1 domain as the autoantigen in Goodpasture syndrome.
